cards.explanation: The answer is her father's house. The text says she left him "…to return to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah." So she went back to where she came from. I think that tells you how things stood between the two of them at that point. Her dad's house is where this whole next stretch of the story happens.

The answer is to speak kindly to her and bring her back. The text says her husband went after her "…to speak kindly to her and bring her back…" That's a long trip with a servant and a pair of donkeys, so he means business. That's what the passage tells us about why he went.

The answer is False. Her father is not unhappy to see him, because the text says he "…gladly welcomed him." The girl brings the Levite into the house, and her dad is glad he's there. That's the whole mood of the scene. Hold on to it, friends, because the story won't stay this warm.

The answer is a bite of bread before he goes. The father says, "Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread, and then you can go." Just a little bread, and then he can leave. Sounds like me with a batch, friends. 'One more cookie' is how every long goodbye starts.

The answer is False. The Levite gets up early to depart, but the father says, "Please refresh your heart." So they wait until late afternoon and eat. Getting up early to leave and still being at the table in late afternoon are two very different things.

The answer is that he leaves anyway with his concubine. The text says "…the man was unwilling to spend the night. He got up and departed…" He leaves with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine, and the servant is still with them. After all those requests from his father-in-law, he finally doesn't stay.

The answer is to stop and spend the night in Jebus. The servant says, "Please, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here." The day is almost gone, so it sounds like a plain, practical idea to me. The text says Jebus is Jerusalem (Judges 19:10). The servant is the one asking here, and the Levite answers him next.

The answer is foreigners. The Levite says, "We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites." He gives his reason right there: no Israelites are in that city. So he tells his servant they'll go on to Gibeah instead.

The answer is True, and it's a hard moment. The sun set as they neared Gibeah, and the Levite went in and sat down in the city square, "…but no one would take them into his home for the night." I think it's a lonely feeling to sit there with nobody opening a door.

The answer is that he asks where the traveler is going and where he came from. The old man says, "Where are you going, and where have you come from?" He has come in from his work in the field and spots the traveler sitting in the square. It's a simple question, and the Levite answers all of it.

The answer is the house of the LORD. The Levite says, "I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD…" He's heading home to Ephraim, and he names that as where he's going too. The text doesn't say more about his plan, so I'll leave it there.

The answer is that he offers to supply everything the Levite needs. The old man says, "Peace to you," and then, "Let me supply everything you need. Only do not spend the night in the square." That's a big, open-handed offer. I think after all those closed doors, it must have sounded like a whole new world. Notice the Levite said he lacked nothing, and the old man still offers to supply what he needs.

The answer is that this man is a guest in his house. The old man says, "After all, this man is a guest in my house." He also calls it a wicked thing and an outrage. I think this is a heavy scene, so I'll just say plainly that the old man tells them to stop.
The answer is False. The men do not listen to him. The text says, "…the men would not listen to him." It's a heavy part of the story, friends. I think it's okay to feel how heavy it is.

The answer is True. The text says that early that morning "…the woman went back to the house where her master was staying, collapsed at the doorway, and lay there until it was light." At dawn the men let her go, and that's where she goes. I think this is one of the hardest verses in the whole book.

The answer is that he tells her to get up and let them go. The text has him say, "Get up," and then, "Let us go." Then it says, "But there was no response." That's all the passage gives us for his words to her. It stays heavy, and I think it's fair to say so.

The answer is throughout the territory of Israel. The text says he cut her into twelve pieces "…and sent her throughout the territory of Israel." It's a grim scene, and I'll keep it simple. What the people say when they see it comes in the next verse.

The answer is Egypt. Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day." They're pointing back to the day the Israelites came out of Egypt. So the people were saying nothing like this had been seen or done in all that time.

The answer is False. They don't say to keep quiet. They say, "Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!" That means think, talk it over and say something. It's a serious moment, and I'd say the people knew it. The story isn't over, though.
